The full answer for this step, with every rule and source
The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?

Where things stand

A motion for summary judgment asks the court to decide all or part of the claim on affidavits or other evidence. When a plaintiff brings it, it asks for judgment on all or part of the claim. When a defendant brings it, it asks that all or part of the claim be dismissed. The court must grant summary judgment if it is satisfied there is no genuine issue that needs a trial on a claim or defence. It must also grant it if the parties agree to have all or part of the claim decided this way, and the court is satisfied that is appropriate.

What to do next

If you are responding, you cannot rest only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, that show there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. An affidavit on this motion may state what the person swearing it was told and believes, if it names the source and says that they believe it. But at the hearing, the court may, if appropriate, draw an adverse inference when a party does not give evidence from a person who has personal knowledge of facts in dispute. On this motion, each party must serve a factum on every other party to the motion, and it must meet the requirements of rule 4.06.1. If you are responding, you must serve your factum and file it with proof of service at the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, you must serve and file your factum the same way at least seven days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, then unless the court orders otherwise, you must also serve a motion record on every other party at least seven days before the hearing. You must file it with proof of service at that court office by the same time. If you are responding, the moving party's motion record holds the affidavits and other material any party has served for use on the motion. The court file is not put before the judge unless the judge asks for it or a party requisitions it. If material you will use on the motion is not in the moving party's motion record, you may put it in a responding party's motion record. Serving and filing it are one step. You serve it on every other party and file it, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and a copy of any material you will use on the motion that is not in the motion record.

Your deadline

If you are bringing the motion for summary judgment, serve the notice of motion, motion record and your factum on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday. You must also give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 2 p.m. five days before the hearing. If you do not, the motion is not heard.

If you are responding to a motion for summary judgment, serve your factum on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. You cannot rely only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, showing there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday.

If you are responding, serve your affidavits and other evidence on the other parties. If the moving party's motion record does not include them, serve and file a responding party's motion record containing them, with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is how your evidence of specific facts reaches the court. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. If the moving party did not email you a copy of their confirmation of motion, you may give the registrar your own confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 10 a.m. four days before the hearing.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

What happens after

To decide if there is a genuine issue that needs a trial, the court must consider the evidence the parties gave. A judge may weigh the evidence and judge how believable a person who swore an affidavit is. The judge may also draw reasonable inferences from the evidence. But a judge does not use these powers if the interest of justice means they should be used only at a trial. For this, a judge may also order one or more parties to give oral evidence, with or without time limits. If summary judgment is refused or granted only in part, the court may set out the facts not in dispute and the issues to be tried. It may also order the case to go to trial quickly. The court may order a party to pay the costs of the motion on a substantial indemnity basis in two cases. One is if the party acted unreasonably in making or responding to the motion. The other is if the party acted in bad faith to cause delay.

The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?

Where things stand

A motion for summary judgment asks the court to decide all or part of the claim on affidavits or other evidence. When a plaintiff brings it, it asks for judgment on all or part of the claim. When a defendant brings it, it asks that all or part of the claim be dismissed. The court must grant summary judgment if it is satisfied there is no genuine issue that needs a trial on a claim or defence. It must also grant it if the parties agree to have all or part of the claim decided this way, and the court is satisfied that is appropriate.

What to do next

If you are responding, you cannot rest only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, that show there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. An affidavit on this motion may state what the person swearing it was told and believes, if it names the source and says that they believe it. But at the hearing, the court may, if appropriate, draw an adverse inference when a party does not give evidence from a person who has personal knowledge of facts in dispute. On this motion, each party must serve a factum on every other party to the motion, and it must meet the requirements of rule 4.06.1. If you are responding, you must serve your factum and file it with proof of service at the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, you must serve and file your factum the same way at least seven days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, then unless the court orders otherwise, you must also serve a motion record on every other party at least seven days before the hearing. You must file it with proof of service at that court office by the same time. If you are responding, the moving party's motion record holds the affidavits and other material any party has served for use on the motion. The court file is not put before the judge unless the judge asks for it or a party requisitions it. If material you will use on the motion is not in the moving party's motion record, you may put it in a responding party's motion record. Serving and filing it are one step. You serve it on every other party and file it, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and a copy of any material you will use on the motion that is not in the motion record.

Your deadline

If you are bringing the motion for summary judgment, serve the notice of motion, motion record and your factum on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday. You must also give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 2 p.m. five days before the hearing. If you do not, the motion is not heard.

If you are responding to a motion for summary judgment, serve your factum on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. You cannot rely only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, showing there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday.

If you are responding, serve your affidavits and other evidence on the other parties. If the moving party's motion record does not include them, serve and file a responding party's motion record containing them, with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is how your evidence of specific facts reaches the court. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. If the moving party did not email you a copy of their confirmation of motion, you may give the registrar your own confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 10 a.m. four days before the hearing.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

What happens after

To decide if there is a genuine issue that needs a trial, the court must consider the evidence the parties gave. A judge may weigh the evidence and judge how believable a person who swore an affidavit is. The judge may also draw reasonable inferences from the evidence. But a judge does not use these powers if the interest of justice means they should be used only at a trial. For this, a judge may also order one or more parties to give oral evidence, with or without time limits. If summary judgment is refused or granted only in part, the court may set out the facts not in dispute and the issues to be tried. It may also order the case to go to trial quickly. The court may order a party to pay the costs of the motion on a substantial indemnity basis in two cases. One is if the party acted unreasonably in making or responding to the motion. The other is if the party acted in bad faith to cause delay.

Stage recorded: I need to bring or answer a motion

Change this
What happens next at your exact step

Based on what you told us, this is your step. If it is not right, choose the question closest to where your case is.

Your step: The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file? Not right? Choose another step

YOUR NEXT STEP

Where you are: A motion for summary judgment is scheduled

If you are bringing the motion for summary judgment, serve the notice of motion, motion record and your factum on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Based on the date you gave us, this has to be done by Tuesday 24 November 2026 at the latest.
If you are responding to a motion for summary judgment, serve your factum on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Based on the date you gave us, this has to be done by Friday 27 November 2026 at the latest.
If you are responding, serve your affidavits and other evidence on the other parties. If the moving party's motion record does not include them, serve and file a responding party's motion record containing them, with proof of service. Based on the date you gave us, this has to be done by Friday 27 November 2026 at the latest.

If you are responding, you cannot rest only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, that show there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. An affidavit on this motion may state what the person swearing it was told and believes, if it names the source and says that they believe it. But at the hearing, the court may, if appropriate, draw an adverse inference when a party does not give evidence from a person who has personal knowledge of facts in dispute. On this motion, each party must serve a factum on every other party to the motion, and it must meet the requirements of rule 4.06.1. If you are responding, you must serve your factum and file it with proof of service at the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, you must serve and file your factum the same way at least seven days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, then unless the court orders otherwise, you must also serve a motion record on every other party at least seven days before the hearing. You must file it with proof of service at that court office by the same time. If you are responding, the moving party's motion record holds the affidavits and other material any party has served for use on the motion. The court file is not put before the judge unless the judge asks for it or a party requisitions it. If material you will use on the motion is not in the moving party's motion record, you may put it in a responding party's motion record. Serving and filing it are one step. You serve it on every other party and file it, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and a copy of any material you will use on the motion that is not in the motion record.

The forms

Form 37A — Notice of MotionPDFWord
Form 37B — Confirmation of MotionWord

From the official Ontario Court Forms site. Check the version date there before you file.

What it costs

Filing a motion (paid by the person bringing it): $339
O. Reg. 293/92 (Superior Court of Justice and Court of Appeal fees), s. 1 (1), para. 3 iv · checked 2026-09-30

“A notice of motion served on another party, a notice of motion without notice, a notice of motion for a consent order or a notice of motion for leave to appeal, other than a notice of motion in a family law appeal, $339.”

If you cannot afford the fee, you can ask the court to waive it. Asking costs nothing.
ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived, Overview · checked 2026-09-27

“If you cannot afford to pay the fees, you can ask the court to waive them. ... There is no cost to apply for a fee waiver.”

Where and how to file

Outside Toronto, file online through the Civil Claims Online or Civil Submissions Online portal.
ontario.ca, File a civil claim online, Overview · checked 2026-09-27

“The Civil Claims Online and Civil Submissions Online portals will continue to be available to file court documents online for civil and Divisional Court cases in other regions outside of Toronto.”

If a deadline is 3 business days away or fewer, you cannot file online for it.
ontario.ca, File a civil claim online, Documents you can file online · checked 2026-09-27

“if you need to meet a deadline established by legislation or other court rules, court practice direction or a court order that is 3 business days or fewer away”

Serving it on the other side

Other documents go to the other side's lawyer if they have one; a person acting for themselves can be served by mail to their last address for service.
Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, r. 16.01 (4) · checked 2026-09-27

“shall be served on a party who has a lawyer of record by serving the lawyer, and service may be made in a manner provided in rule 16.05; (b) may be served on a party acting in person or on a person who is not a party, (i) by mailing a copy of the document to the last address for service provided by the party or other person or, if no such address has been provided, to the party's or person's last known address”

Prove service with an affidavit of service (Form 16B) from whoever served it.
Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, r. 16.09 (1) · checked 2026-09-27

“Service of a document may be proved by an affidavit of the person who served it (Form 16B).”

The rule for this step

“A motion shall be made by a notice of motion (in Form 37A) unless the nature of the motion or the circumstances make a notice of motion unnecessary or these rules provide otherwise.”
Rules of Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, r. 37.01 · checked 2026-09-27

The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?

Where things stand

A motion for summary judgment asks the court to decide all or part of the claim on affidavits or other evidence. When a plaintiff brings it, it asks for judgment on all or part of the claim. When a defendant brings it, it asks that all or part of the claim be dismissed. The court must grant summary judgment if it is satisfied there is no genuine issue that needs a trial on a claim or defence. It must also grant it if the parties agree to have all or part of the claim decided this way, and the court is satisfied that is appropriate.

What to do next

If you are responding, you cannot rest only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, that show there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. An affidavit on this motion may state what the person swearing it was told and believes, if it names the source and says that they believe it. But at the hearing, the court may, if appropriate, draw an adverse inference when a party does not give evidence from a person who has personal knowledge of facts in dispute. On this motion, each party must serve a factum on every other party to the motion, and it must meet the requirements of rule 4.06.1. If you are responding, you must serve your factum and file it with proof of service at the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, you must serve and file your factum the same way at least seven days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, then unless the court orders otherwise, you must also serve a motion record on every other party at least seven days before the hearing. You must file it with proof of service at that court office by the same time. If you are responding, the moving party's motion record holds the affidavits and other material any party has served for use on the motion. The court file is not put before the judge unless the judge asks for it or a party requisitions it. If material you will use on the motion is not in the moving party's motion record, you may put it in a responding party's motion record. Serving and filing it are one step. You serve it on every other party and file it, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and a copy of any material you will use on the motion that is not in the motion record.

Your deadline

If you are bringing the motion for summary judgment, serve the notice of motion, motion record and your factum on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday. You must also give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 2 p.m. five days before the hearing. If you do not, the motion is not heard.

If you are responding to a motion for summary judgment, serve your factum on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. You cannot rely only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, showing there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday.

If you are responding, serve your affidavits and other evidence on the other parties. If the moving party's motion record does not include them, serve and file a responding party's motion record containing them, with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is how your evidence of specific facts reaches the court. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. If the moving party did not email you a copy of their confirmation of motion, you may give the registrar your own confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 10 a.m. four days before the hearing.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

What happens after

To decide if there is a genuine issue that needs a trial, the court must consider the evidence the parties gave. A judge may weigh the evidence and judge how believable a person who swore an affidavit is. The judge may also draw reasonable inferences from the evidence. But a judge does not use these powers if the interest of justice means they should be used only at a trial. For this, a judge may also order one or more parties to give oral evidence, with or without time limits. If summary judgment is refused or granted only in part, the court may set out the facts not in dispute and the issues to be tried. It may also order the case to go to trial quickly. The court may order a party to pay the costs of the motion on a substantial indemnity basis in two cases. One is if the party acted unreasonably in making or responding to the motion. The other is if the party acted in bad faith to cause delay.

The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?

Where things stand

A motion for summary judgment asks the court to decide all or part of the claim on affidavits or other evidence. When a plaintiff brings it, it asks for judgment on all or part of the claim. When a defendant brings it, it asks that all or part of the claim be dismissed. The court must grant summary judgment if it is satisfied there is no genuine issue that needs a trial on a claim or defence. It must also grant it if the parties agree to have all or part of the claim decided this way, and the court is satisfied that is appropriate.

What to do next

If you are responding, you cannot rest only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, that show there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. An affidavit on this motion may state what the person swearing it was told and believes, if it names the source and says that they believe it. But at the hearing, the court may, if appropriate, draw an adverse inference when a party does not give evidence from a person who has personal knowledge of facts in dispute. On this motion, each party must serve a factum on every other party to the motion, and it must meet the requirements of rule 4.06.1. If you are responding, you must serve your factum and file it with proof of service at the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, you must serve and file your factum the same way at least seven days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, then unless the court orders otherwise, you must also serve a motion record on every other party at least seven days before the hearing. You must file it with proof of service at that court office by the same time. If you are responding, the moving party's motion record holds the affidavits and other material any party has served for use on the motion. The court file is not put before the judge unless the judge asks for it or a party requisitions it. If material you will use on the motion is not in the moving party's motion record, you may put it in a responding party's motion record. Serving and filing it are one step. You serve it on every other party and file it, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and a copy of any material you will use on the motion that is not in the motion record.

Your deadline

If you are bringing the motion for summary judgment, serve the notice of motion, motion record and your factum on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday. You must also give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 2 p.m. five days before the hearing. If you do not, the motion is not heard.

If you are responding to a motion for summary judgment, serve your factum on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. You cannot rely only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, showing there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday.

If you are responding, serve your affidavits and other evidence on the other parties. If the moving party's motion record does not include them, serve and file a responding party's motion record containing them, with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is how your evidence of specific facts reaches the court. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. If the moving party did not email you a copy of their confirmation of motion, you may give the registrar your own confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 10 a.m. four days before the hearing.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

What happens after

To decide if there is a genuine issue that needs a trial, the court must consider the evidence the parties gave. A judge may weigh the evidence and judge how believable a person who swore an affidavit is. The judge may also draw reasonable inferences from the evidence. But a judge does not use these powers if the interest of justice means they should be used only at a trial. For this, a judge may also order one or more parties to give oral evidence, with or without time limits. If summary judgment is refused or granted only in part, the court may set out the facts not in dispute and the issues to be tried. It may also order the case to go to trial quickly. The court may order a party to pay the costs of the motion on a substantial indemnity basis in two cases. One is if the party acted unreasonably in making or responding to the motion. The other is if the party acted in bad faith to cause delay.

The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?

Where things stand

A motion for summary judgment asks the court to decide all or part of the claim on affidavits or other evidence. When a plaintiff brings it, it asks for judgment on all or part of the claim. When a defendant brings it, it asks that all or part of the claim be dismissed. The court must grant summary judgment if it is satisfied there is no genuine issue that needs a trial on a claim or defence. It must also grant it if the parties agree to have all or part of the claim decided this way, and the court is satisfied that is appropriate.

What to do next

If you are responding, you cannot rest only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, that show there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. An affidavit on this motion may state what the person swearing it was told and believes, if it names the source and says that they believe it. But at the hearing, the court may, if appropriate, draw an adverse inference when a party does not give evidence from a person who has personal knowledge of facts in dispute. On this motion, each party must serve a factum on every other party to the motion, and it must meet the requirements of rule 4.06.1. If you are responding, you must serve your factum and file it with proof of service at the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, you must serve and file your factum the same way at least seven days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, then unless the court orders otherwise, you must also serve a motion record on every other party at least seven days before the hearing. You must file it with proof of service at that court office by the same time. If you are responding, the moving party's motion record holds the affidavits and other material any party has served for use on the motion. The court file is not put before the judge unless the judge asks for it or a party requisitions it. If material you will use on the motion is not in the moving party's motion record, you may put it in a responding party's motion record. Serving and filing it are one step. You serve it on every other party and file it, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and a copy of any material you will use on the motion that is not in the motion record.

Your deadline

If you are bringing the motion for summary judgment, serve the notice of motion, motion record and your factum on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday. You must also give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 2 p.m. five days before the hearing. If you do not, the motion is not heard.

If you are responding to a motion for summary judgment, serve your factum on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. You cannot rely only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, showing there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday.

If you are responding, serve your affidavits and other evidence on the other parties. If the moving party's motion record does not include them, serve and file a responding party's motion record containing them, with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is how your evidence of specific facts reaches the court. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. If the moving party did not email you a copy of their confirmation of motion, you may give the registrar your own confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 10 a.m. four days before the hearing.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

What happens after

To decide if there is a genuine issue that needs a trial, the court must consider the evidence the parties gave. A judge may weigh the evidence and judge how believable a person who swore an affidavit is. The judge may also draw reasonable inferences from the evidence. But a judge does not use these powers if the interest of justice means they should be used only at a trial. For this, a judge may also order one or more parties to give oral evidence, with or without time limits. If summary judgment is refused or granted only in part, the court may set out the facts not in dispute and the issues to be tried. It may also order the case to go to trial quickly. The court may order a party to pay the costs of the motion on a substantial indemnity basis in two cases. One is if the party acted unreasonably in making or responding to the motion. The other is if the party acted in bad faith to cause delay.
